analysis.one_liner: Taxes soda makers a penny per teaspoon of sugar to fund diabetes and obesity prevention programs.
analysis.headline: The soda-tax bill never got a hearing or a vote in either committee; it sat for two years until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SWEET Act would put a federal excise tax on sugary drinks, charged to manufacturers at one cent for every 4.2 grams of added sweetener, and adjusted up with inflation. The money would go to the Prevention and Public Health Fund specifically for programs and research to fight diabetes, obesity, and tooth decay in the communities hit hardest. Sponsors pointed to evidence that sugary drinks drive obesity, which falls disproportionately on low-income people and communities of color. The bill never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: People at high risk of diet-related disease, especially low-income households and communities of color, who would gain from funded prevention, treatment, and research programs. Public health programs would gain a dedicated new funding stream. The tax is also designed to nudge people away from heavy soda consumption, which sponsors cited as a driver of weight gain and diabetes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing diabetes and obesity risk

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on sugar-sweetened beverages, charged to the manufacturer, producer, or importer, at a rate of one cent per 4.2 grams of caloric sweetener, with the rate rising with inflation after 2015.

Dedicates all revenue from the tax to the Prevention and Public Health Fund, restricted to programs and research aimed at reducing the human and economic costs of diabetes, obesity, dental caries, and other diet-related conditions in priority populations.
Exempts milk, plant-based milks, pure fruit and vegetable juices, infant formula, and medically necessary nutritional drinks, so the tax targets added-sugar drinks rather than staple foods.

The bill's findings cite large racial and income disparities: in 2012, 47.8% of African-American adults and 42.5% of Hispanic adults were obese, and obesity costs an estimated $190 billion a year, over 20% of it paid publicly through Medicare and Medicaid.

analysis.who_pays: Sugary drink manufacturers pay the tax directly, and consumers would likely bear much of it in higher prices, including low-income households that buy the most soda. Beverage companies lose sales if the tax succeeds in curbing demand.
analysis.who_pays_short: Soda makers and heavy soda drinkers

drawbacks.text: Soda taxes are regressive in design: low-income households spend a larger share of their income on soda, so they pay more of the tax, unless the health effects and funded programs offset that over time.
The tax's health benefit depends on people actually drinking less; drinkers can switch to untaxed products, so the revenue and the health gains are both uncertain.
The tax is defined by grams of sweetener per product, a structure that requires detailed measurement across thousands of drink formulas and creates administrative complexity for manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is strong on paper: it targets a product with documented links to obesity and diabetes, exempts staples, and dedicates the money to the communities bearing the worst of the disease burden. The honest cost is that the tax falls partly on the very low-income consumers it aims to help, and its benefits depend on unproven changes in buying behavior. A fair assessment is that it is a well-designed version of a policy tool with real distributional trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee on day two, and neither committee ever acted on it, so it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 26, 2015, joined by Reps. Norton and Rush; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and also to Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Health subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill is recorded in its action history for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew only four cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugary beverage makers and corn syrup producers kept operating with no new federal tax, and soda drinkers paid no higher prices. The communities with high rates of diabetes and obesity did not get the dedicated prevention funding the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Soda makers and corn syrup producers

sides.party_line_note: All five House backers (the sponsor plus four cosponsors) were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call breakdown.

industries.note: The tax is charged directly to manufacturers, importers, and producers of sweetened drinks and is explicitly designed to shrink demand for their core products. Beverage companies fought soda taxes across the country during this period, and their commercial interest in keeping soda cheap runs against the public health goal of the bill.

The tax applies to high-fructose corn syrup and other caloric sweeteners in beverages, hitting the makers and buyers of those ingredients. Their interest was in avoiding a levy that would reduce beverage production.

industries.industry: Public health programs and community health providers
industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated stream of funding for diabetes, obesity, and dental disease programs in the hardest-hit populations. These groups win or lose together with the communities they serve.
